sentences.text: Tenontosaurus was a medium-sized ornithopod dinosaur that measured between 6.5 and 8 meters in length, stood 2.2 meters tall, and weighed approximately 1000 kg, though estimates suggest a weight range up to 2 tons.

Its head featured a thick, U-shaped beak formed by flaring premaxillae, which worked with a lower jaw ending in a predentary bone to create a unique lower beak structure characteristic of ornithischians.
The skull was low and long, appearing very elongated when viewed from above, and contained teeth that were enameled on only the inner or medial surface.

Its spine consisted of twelve cervical vertebrae, fifteen dorsal vertebrae, six sacral vertebrae, and at least sixty-one tail vertebrae, supporting a long, broad tail and a stiff back held by a network of bony tendons.
Populations of Tenontosaurus increased dramatically during a shift from arid to wetter climates, demonstrating it was a remarkably adaptable animal.

Like Tyrannosaurus and Allosaurus, this individual Tenontosaurus did not reach full adult size before dying at 8 years old, a pattern suggesting that early-diverging dinosaur lineages reached reproductive maturity before achieving maximum size.
Medullary bone tissue found in the femur and tibia of a specimen indicates that Tenontosaurus used this tissue, found today only in egg-laying birds, for reproduction.

The first fossil of Tenontosaurus was discovered in 1903 in Big Horn County, Montana, by an AMNH expedition, leading Barnum Brown to informally name the animal 'Tenantosaurus' or 'sinew lizard' due to its stiffening tendons.
The genus Tenontosaurus was formally named by John Ostrom in 1970.
In 2013, Jonathan Tennant described the postcranial skeleton using specimen LL.12275, and in 2015, the skull was described in detail using a new specimen, OMNH 58340, which was found in 2000.
Tenontosaurus was a facultative quadruped capable of standing on two or four legs, likely using a quadrupedal stance for feeding but probably unable to move rapidly on four legs.

As a low browser, an adult Tenontosaurus could reach a maximum height of about 3 meters when standing bipedally, allowing it to consume leaves, wood, and fruit with its powerful U-shaped beak and angled teeth.

Fossil teeth and skeletons of the theropod Deinonychus are frequently found associated with Tenontosaurus tilletti remains, and approximately 20% of Tenontosaurus fossils are found near Deinonychus, leading some scientists to suggest Deinonychus was its major predator.
In the Cloverly Formation, Tenontosaurus was the most abundant vertebrate, five times more common than the next most frequent species, Sauropelta.
In the arid Little Sheep Mudstone Member, Tenontosaurus was the sole herbivorous dinosaur, sharing its habitat with Deinonychus, an allosauroid theropod, and a goniopholid crocodile.
Tenontosaurus is classified as a genus of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur.

Tenontosaurus was originally placed in the family Iguanodontidae but later reclassified into Hypsilophodontidae, although detailed examination suggests it is likely a basal member of Iguanodontia despite its light structure resembling a hypsilophodontid.

When Tenontosaurus first appeared in Wyoming and Montana, the climate was arid to semi-arid with seasonal rainfall and occasional droughts, though it also lived in paleoenvironments of tropical or sub-tropical forests, floodplains, and swamps similar to modern-day Louisiana.

It is debated whether Ostrom's original reconstruction of the Tenontosaurus skull accurately represented its true depth, and the position of Tenontosaurus in the evolutionary tree was very problematic and controversial due to a lack of adequate cladistic analysis.
